dc.e: Lie on the bench, eyes under the bar, feet planted on the floor. Squeeze your shoulder blades together and keep them squeezed from the start to the end of the set. Lower the bar to the bottom of your chest with your elbows at about 45° from your torso, touch your chest without bouncing, then press toward a point above your shoulders.
err: Elbows flared to 90°, which crushes the shoulder joint without recruiting any more chest.
Shoulder blades relaxing from the second rep, which costs you your base and your power.
Hips lifting off the bench, a sign the load exceeds what your range of motion allows.
dc.p: This exercise is capped at RPE 8 for the whole cycle, even in week 8: without a spotter, grinding out the last rep under a bar is the only place in the program where failure is dangerous. Always keep two reps in reserve.

dh.e: A dumbbell in each hand, shoulder blades squeezed, feet on the floor. Lower until the dumbbells reach chest height, elbows at 45°, then press while bringing your hands slightly together without clanking them.
err: Lowering the dumbbells too far and straining the front of the shoulder.
Flaring the elbows to 90° from the torso.
dh.p: The range of motion is bigger than with the bar, so the load will be lower: that's normal, don't compare the two. When the set comes out below the target RPE, go up one dumbbell.

pomp.e: Hands slightly wider than your shoulders, body in a line from heels to head, glutes squeezed. Lower until your chest brushes the floor, elbows going back rather than out to the sides, then push without breaking the line of your hips.
err: Sagging hips, which shifts the load onto the lower back.
Only going halfway down, which removes the most useful part of the movement.
pomp.p: Once you go past 15 reps at RPE 8, progress comes from difficulty, not numbers: feet elevated, then weight on your back.

dip.e: Parallel bars, arms straight, torso leaning slightly forward to target the chest. Lower until your shoulder reaches elbow level, no lower, then come back up by fully straightening your arms.
err: Going too low, which puts the shoulder in a vulnerable position.
Staying perfectly upright, which shifts all the work onto the triceps.
dip.p: Bodyweight first. When you can do 3 sets of 10 at RPE 8, add 2.5 kg on a belt.

dm.e: Bar on your upper chest, hands just outside your shoulders, elbows slightly forward. Squeeze your glutes and abs to lock your pelvis, then press straight up, moving your head back slightly to let the bar pass. At the top, arms straight, bar above the middle of your head.
err: Arching the lower back to make up for a lack of shoulder mobility.
Pushing the bar forward rather than straight up.
Finishing with arms straight but the bar still in front of your face, which keeps the shoulder under constant tension.
dm.p: If you reported shoulder discomfort, stay at RPE 7 while it lasts, whatever the week of the cycle. Clean range of motion comes before load.

dmh.e: Seated with an upright backrest or standing, dumbbells at ear height, palms facing forward. Press straight up without clanking the dumbbells at the top, then lower until your elbows pass below shoulder level.
err: Flaring the elbows backward, which strains the shoulder.
Cutting the descent short and only working the top of the movement.
dmh.p: Easier on the shoulders than the bar, because your hands follow their natural path. Go up one step when the set comes out below the target RPE.

pv3.e: Feet against a wall, hands slightly wider than your shoulders, core braced. Lower under control until the top of your head brushes the floor, then press straight up.
err: Arching the back to make up for a lack of strength.
Lowering too fast and hitting your head on the floor.
pv3.p: A demanding exercise. Start with your feet on a chair rather than the wall, and only add range once you can do 3 sets of 8.

tr.e: Grip slightly wider than your shoulders, palms facing forward. Start by pulling your shoulders down before bending your arms: the movement starts from the back, not the hands. Pull up until your chin clears the bar, then lower under control to straight arms.
err: Starting from straight arms without pulling the shoulders down, which turns the exercise into a biceps pull.
Cutting the descent short and bouncing back up.
Swinging the legs to start the pull when fatigue sets in.
tr.p: Progress with added weight. When sets come out below the target RPE, add 2.5 kg on a belt rather than more reps.

tp.e: Thighs locked under the pads, wide grip. First pull your shoulders down, then pull the bar to your upper chest by driving your elbows down and back. Return under control to a full stretch.
err: Leaning far back to pull heavier.
Pulling behind the neck, which puts the shoulder in extreme rotation.
tp.p: The right fallback when pull-ups no longer come out cleanly at the end of a workout. Go up one pin when the set falls below the target RPE.

rw.e: Torso bent at about 45°, back flat, bar hanging at arm's length. Pull the bar toward your navel by driving your elbows back, squeeze your shoulder blades for half a second, then lower under control without letting your torso rise.
err: Gradually standing up over the reps until you finish almost upright.
Pulling with the biceps while keeping the elbows tucked against the body.
Rounding the upper back on the way down.
rw.p: Make a clear pause at the top of each rep: that's what separates a row from a swing. Add 2.5 kg when the set comes out below the target RPE with the pause held.

rh.e: One hand and one knee on the bench, back flat and parallel to the floor. Pull the dumbbell toward your hip by driving your elbow back, then lower to a full stretch without rotating your torso.
err: Twisting the torso to build momentum.
Pulling toward the shoulder rather than the hip.
rh.p: Much easier on the lower back than the barbell row. Choose it if you reported lower back discomfort.

ra.e: Bar at hip height, hanging underneath, body in a line, heels on the floor. Pull your chest to the bar while squeezing your shoulder blades, then lower to straight arms without breaking the line of your hips.
err: Hips sagging on the way up.
Pulling your belly rather than your chest to the bar.
ra.p: To make it harder, lower the bar or raise your feet rather than adding reps past fifteen.

sq.e: Bar on your upper traps, hands at a comfortable width, elbows under the bar. Breathe in, brace, then descend by pushing your knees out and your hips back. Aim at least for thighs parallel to the floor, then stand up by pushing the floor away with your whole foot.
err: Heels lifting, often a lack of ankle mobility that heeled shoes fix immediately.
Knees caving inward on the way up.
Stopping well above parallel with a heavy load, which gives the illusion of progress.
sq.p: Range of motion comes before load: a set at RPE 8 going below parallel is worth more than a shortened set at RPE 9. Film yourself from the side once per cycle to check.

pr.e: Back and hips pressed against the backrest, feet hip-width apart in the middle of the platform. Lower until your knees reach about 90°, without your lower back lifting off, then push without violently locking your knees.
err: Going so low that the pelvis tucks and lifts off the backrest.
Snapping the legs straight at the end of the push.
pr.p: Careful: the load shown is not comparable from one machine to another. That's exactly why the program thinks in RPE rather than kilos.

fe.e: A dumbbell in each hand, torso upright. Take a long step forward and lower until your back knee nearly touches the floor, then push off with your front leg to come back. Alternate legs.
err: Taking too short a step, which pushes the front knee far past the toes.
Leaning forward on the way up.
fe.p: Single-leg work: count reps per leg. Useful to fix a left-right imbalance that the squat hides.

rm.e: Start standing, bar against your thighs, knees slightly bent and locked in that position. Push your hips back, letting the bar slide down your legs, back flat. Lower until you feel the stretch in your hamstrings, usually at mid-shin, then come back up by driving your hips forward.
err: Bending the knees on the way down, which turns it into a conventional deadlift and takes tension off the hamstrings.
Rounding the lower back while trying to go lower than your flexibility allows.
Letting the bar drift away from the legs, which multiplies the stress on the lower back.
rm.p: The marker isn't the floor but the stretch: stop the descent where your back would start to round. Add 5 kg when the set comes out below the target RPE without losing position.

ht.e: Upper back against a bench, bar on the hip crease with a pad, feet flat. Drive your hips up until shoulders, hips and knees line up, hold for one second while squeezing your glutes, then lower under control.
err: Going into lower back hyperextension instead of stopping at alignment.
Feet too far out, which shifts the work onto the hamstrings.
ht.p: The pause at the top matters more than the load. A full second on every rep before you consider adding plates.

el.e: Standing, dumbbells by your sides, elbows very slightly bent. Raise your arms out to the sides to shoulder height, leading with your elbows rather than your hands. Lower slowly, over about two seconds.
err: Going too heavy and swinging the weight up with your torso.
Raising above shoulder level, which shifts the work onto the traps.
Letting the arms drop without control.
el.p: Here the load matters little and the effort scale matters a lot. Try to add reps at the same weight before going up one dumbbell.

fp.e: Cable set at face height, rope in a neutral grip. Pull toward your forehead while spreading your hands, elbows high and in line with your shoulders. Finish in external rotation, hands above elbows, then return under control.
err: Pulling too low, toward the chest, which turns it into a back row.
Letting the elbows drop below shoulder level.
Going heavy and losing the external rotation, which is the whole point of the movement.
fp.p: A shoulder health movement, to keep around RPE 7 even at the end of the cycle. This is not an exercise where you look for your limit.

cu.e: Bench inclined at 45°, arms hanging behind the line of your body. Curl the dumbbell without moving your elbow forward, turning your wrist slightly outward at the top. Lower to fully straight arms.
err: Moving the elbows forward to finish the rep, which takes tension off the biceps.
Cutting the descent short and losing the stretch, which is the whole point of the incline position.
Lifting your back off the bench to swing the weight.
cu.p: Add only 1 kg when all three sets come out below the target RPE without the elbows moving forward. If you stall, slow the descent to three seconds before going heavier: the biceps responds better to time under tension than to load.

tri.e: Standing facing the high pulley, elbows pinned to your torso and still. Extend your arms to a full lockout, pause, then come back up under control without letting your elbows flare.
err: Leaning the torso forward to push with your body weight.
Letting the elbows drift back on the way up.
Not locking the arms at the bottom, where the triceps works hardest.
Letting the cable pull you back up, which removes the whole return phase.
tri.p: Go up one pin when the last set stays below the target RPE with your elbows still. Keep in mind that the triceps makes up two thirds of the arm's volume: if you want bigger arms, this is where it happens, more than with curls.

gai.e: On your forearms and toes, elbows under your shoulders. Tuck your pelvis to flatten the arch, squeeze your glutes, and keep a straight line from shoulders to heels. Breathe normally.
err: Hips too high, which turns the position into a rest.
Lower back sagging, which shifts the stress onto the lower back.
Holding your breath instead of breathing normally.
Chasing performance by holding for three minutes: beyond a clean minute, you're training position endurance, not core strength.
gai.p: Abs aren't programmed like a bench press: your squat and deadlift already work them hard. Here we just add what's missing. Move to 60 seconds once your pelvis no longer moves.

rj.e: Hanging from the bar, shoulders down and active. Curl your pelvis up before raising your legs, as if bringing your pubic bone toward your sternum. Lower slowly without letting your body swing.
err: Raising the legs without curling the pelvis, which only works the hip flexors.
Swinging to start the lift.
Dropping the legs in free fall, which arches the lower back.
rj.p: Knees bent first. Move to straight legs once three sets come out without swinging, before adding reps.

lom.e: Hips on the pad, feet locked, torso free. Lower under control until your torso is vertical, back neutral, then come up while squeezing your glutes until you're in line with your legs, no further.
err: Going into hyperextension past alignment, which compresses the lower back.
Rounding the back on the way down instead of hinging at the hip.
Using momentum on every rep.
lom.p: Often forgotten by those who stall on the deadlift. Bodyweight first, then a 5 kg plate against your chest.

ram.e: Start with legs bent, arms straight, back straight. Push with your legs first, then lean your torso back, and only at the end pull with your arms. The return happens in reverse order: arms, torso, legs.
err: Pulling with the arms first, which exhausts the upper body without producing power.
Rounding the back at the end of the return, the costliest mistake for the lower back.
Starting too hard on the first interval and collapsing on the next ones.
Setting the resistance to maximum thinking you'll work harder: a setting between 3 and 5 matches real rowing and tires the back much less.
ram.p: Note your time on the first interval and aim for the same on the next seven. If the eighth is more than five seconds slower, you started too fast. Consistency is the only indicator that matters here, and it's also what keeps this workout from eating into your leg workouts.

hip.e: One knee on the floor, the other foot in front at 90°. Tuck your pelvis under you rather than leaning forward, then shift your weight slightly forward until you feel the stretch in front of the back thigh. Squeeze the glute on the stretched side.
err: Leaning forward and arching the back, which completely cancels the stretch.
Not squeezing the glute on the stretched side, even though that's what actually opens the hip.
Forcing in jerks instead of holding the position while breathing.
Putting the knee straight on a hard floor, which makes you cut the hold short from discomfort rather than lack of flexibility.
hip.p: Best done the day after a leg workout or your other sport, when the hips are tight. No effort level here: you hold and breathe. It's often what's missing for those who can't squat to parallel: the restriction is in front of the hip, not behind.

tho.e: On all fours, hands under your shoulders and knees under your hips. Round your back toward the ceiling, tucking your chin and pelvis, one vertebra at a time, then reverse by arching your upper back and opening your chest. The movement should come from the upper back, not the lower back.
err: Going fast and turning the exercise into a rocking motion, when the range comes from time spent at the end positions.
Arching only the lower back, which leaves the upper back as stiff as before.
Holding your breath instead of breathing out as you round.
Placing the hands wider than shoulder width, which shifts the work onto the shoulders.
tho.p: Two sets of ten slow repetitions, holding one second in each end position. It's the movement that most often unlocks the overhead press: when the upper back doesn't extend, the shoulder compensates and the bar drifts forward.

dci.e: Bench inclined between 30 and 45°, no more, or the movement turns into a shoulder press. Lower the bar high on the chest, just under the collarbones, then press straight up.
err: Inclining the bench to 60° or more, which shifts all the work onto the shoulders.
Lowering the bar too low, to the sternum, which breaks the bar path.
Lifting the shoulders off the bench at the end of the set.
dci.p: Expect about 70% of your flat bench press load. Capped at RPE 8 without a spotter, like every movement under a bar.

dhi.e: Bench at 30°, dumbbells at chest height, elbows at 45° from your torso. Press while bringing the dumbbells slightly together, without clanking them, then lower until you feel the stretch.
err: Flaring the elbows out wide, which puts the shoulder in a vulnerable position.
Clanking the dumbbells at the top, which releases the tension.
Arching to help the press.
dhi.p: The descent can go lower than with the bar: that's the whole point. Look for range before kilos.

ecart.e: Standing between two high pulleys, torso leaning slightly forward, elbows fixed and barely bent. Bring your hands together in front of you, thinking about squeezing your chest, then return under control to the stretch.
err: Bending the elbows during the movement, which turns it into a disguised press.
Going heavy and compensating with your whole body.
Cutting the return short and losing the stretch under tension.
ecart.p: An isolation movement: the load matters little, the feel matters a lot. Stay light and look for clean reps.

arn.e: Seated, dumbbells in front of your face, palms toward you. Press while rotating your wrists outward, finishing with arms straight and palms facing forward. Return by reversing the rotation.
err: Rotating the wrists too early, which removes the point of the movement.
Going too heavy and losing the rotation.
Arching the lower back at the end of the set.
arn.p: The rotation is the movement, not a detail. Use noticeably less weight than on a regular shoulder press.

trs.e: Palms toward you, hands shoulder-width apart. Pull your shoulders down, then pull until your chin clears the bar, keeping your elbows close to your body. Lower to straight arms.
err: Swinging to start the pull.
Stopping before the chin, which removes the hardest part.
Neglecting the descent.
trs.p: Easier than overhand pull-ups thanks to the biceps' help. A good fallback when regular pull-ups no longer come out.

tpn.e: V-handle, neutral grip, thighs locked in. Pull your shoulders down, then pull the handle to your upper abdomen, elbows along your sides. Return under control to a full stretch.
err: Leaning back to pull heavier.
Pulling with the arms without engaging the back.
Letting the weight pull you back up.
tpn.p: The neutral grip spares the shoulder and elbow: choose it if you reported discomfort.

tps.e: Seated, knees slightly bent, back straight. Pull the handle toward your navel while squeezing your shoulder blades, without leaning back, then return to straight arms keeping your back flat.
err: Rocking the torso back and forth to pull.
Rounding the back on the return.
Shrugging the shoulders during the pull.
tps.p: Much easier on the lower back than the barbell row at the same load. Go up one pin when the pause at the end of the pull still holds.

rw2.e: Torso bent at 45°, back flat, a dumbbell in each hand. Pull both toward your hips by driving your elbows back, then lower to straight arms without raising your torso.
err: Standing up gradually over the reps.
Pulling toward the shoulders rather than the hips.
Rounding the upper back.
rw2.p: Demands more core stability than the one-arm version. If your lower back tires before your back muscles, switch to the one-arm row.

fb.e: Bar on your traps, torso upright. Take a long step forward and lower until your back knee nearly touches the floor, then push back with the front leg. Alternate sides.
err: Taking too short a step, which pushes the front knee past the toes.
Leaning the torso forward on the way up.
Placing the foot too far inward, which throws off your balance.
fb.p: Count reps per leg. An excellent way to reveal a left-right imbalance that the squat completely hides.

lext.e: Seated, back against the backrest, machine pivot aligned with your knee. Extend your legs to lockout, pause, then lower slowly without letting the weight drop.
err: Setting the pivot too high or too low, which pulls on the knee.
Using your hips for momentum.
Letting the weight drop on the way down.
lext.p: Pure isolation: stay light and look for the hold at the top. Useful to finish a leg workout without loading the spine.

sqf.e: Bar resting on the front of your shoulders, elbows very high and pointing forward. Descend keeping your torso as upright as possible, then stand up by pushing the floor away.
err: Letting the elbows drop, which tips the bar forward.
Leaning forward like in a back squat.
Loading it like a back squat: count on about 75% of it.
sqf.p: Much more demanding for the core and wrist mobility. Choose it if the regular squat bothers your lower back.

lc.e: Lying face down, roller just above your heels, hips pressed down. Bend your knees to bring your heels toward your glutes, pause, then lower slowly.
err: Lifting the hips to help, which arches the back.
Cutting the range short at the top.
Letting the weight drop.
lc.p: Complements the Romanian deadlift: one works the hip, the other the knee. Both are needed for complete hamstrings.

gm.e: Bar on your traps, knees slightly bent and locked. Push your hips back while leaning your torso forward, back flat, to about horizontal, then return by driving your hips forward.
err: Rounding the back, the most dangerous mistake here.
Going heavy: this movement is trained light.
Bending the knees on the way down.
gm.p: Stay very light, around 30% of your Romanian deadlift. It's a strengthening movement, not a performance one.

sdt.e: Bar over the middle of your foot, shins nearly touching it. Grip the bar with straight arms, chest up and back flat, then push the floor away with your legs, keeping the bar against your legs until your hips lock out.
err: Pulling with the back before the legs have pushed.
Letting the bar drift away from the shins.
Hyperextending the back at the end of the movement.
sdt.p: The most recovery-costly movement in the program. Capped at RPE 8: a rep to failure on the deadlift is the best way to lose three weeks.

elf.e: Standing, dumbbells in front of your thighs. Raise one straight arm in front of you to shoulder height, no higher, then lower under control. Alternate.
err: Arching and swinging the torso to lift the weight.
Raising above the shoulder, which adds nothing.
Going too heavy on an isolation movement.
elf.p: The front delts are already heavily worked by every press. Only add this if your shoulders are a declared priority.

rmf.e: Seated facing the backrest, chest against it, arms straight in front. Spread your arms backward leading with the elbows, squeeze for a second, then return under control.
err: Bending the elbows and turning the movement into a row.
Going heavy and compensating with the traps.
Lifting the chest off the pad.
rmf.p: The rear delts are the most often neglected group, and the one that balances all your pressing. High volume, low load.

rot.e: Lying on your side, elbow pinned to your hip and bent at 90°. Rotate your forearm toward the ceiling without lifting the elbow, then lower slowly.
err: Lifting the elbow off the body, which works something else.
Using more than a few kilos: this muscle is tiny.
Going fast instead of controlling.
rot.p: A shoulder health movement, to keep around RPE 6. Two or three kilos are enough, and that's normal.

curlb.e: Standing, bar in an underhand grip at shoulder width, elbows pinned to your torso. Curl the bar without moving your elbows forward or leaning back, then lower to straight arms.
err: Swinging the torso to start the lift, the most common mistake in the gym.
Moving the elbows forward at the top.
Not fully straightening the arms at the bottom.
curlb.p: If you have to swing to finish, it's too heavy. An EZ bar eases the wrists if you have discomfort.

mart.e: Standing, dumbbells in a neutral grip, thumbs up. Curl without rotating your wrist or moving your elbow forward, then lower to straight arms. Alternate arms.
err: Rotating the wrist, which turns it into a regular curl.
Swinging the dumbbells.
Cutting the descent short.
mart.p: Works the brachialis, under the biceps, which pushes the biceps up and thickens the arm. Complementary to the regular curl, not redundant.

pup.e: Armpits set on the preacher pad, arms flat on the support. Curl the bar to halfway, then lower slowly until your arms are almost straight, without snapping them locked.
err: Snapping the arms straight at the bottom, which puts the elbow at risk.
Lifting the armpits off the pad.
Curling too high, where the tension disappears.
pup.p: The preacher pad removes all cheating: that's its point and its difficulty. Use noticeably less weight than a standing curl.

dipt.e: Parallel bars, torso as upright as possible and elbows tucked along your body. Lower until your shoulder reaches elbow level, then come back up by fully straightening your arms.
err: Leaning the torso forward, which shifts the work onto the chest.
Going too low.
Not locking the arms at the top.
dipt.p: The most productive bodyweight triceps movement. Add weight once three sets of ten come out cleanly.

nuq.e: Back to the pulley, rope behind your head, elbows high and pointing forward. Extend your arms upward without moving your elbows, then return under control to the stretch.
err: Letting the elbows flare outward.
Leaning too far forward, which shifts the load.
Cutting the stretch short at the bottom, which is the whole point of the position.
nuq.p: The only position that truly stretches the triceps' long head, the one that gives the arm its thickness. Prefer it to low-pulley extensions if you're after size.

bdips.e: Hands on the edge of a bench behind you, legs straight in front. Lower by bending your elbows backward to 90°, then come back up by straightening your arms.
err: Going too low, which puts the shoulder in extreme internal rotation.
Flaring the elbows.
Helping with the legs by pushing through the heels.
bdips.p: The fallback when no parallel bars are available. Put your feet up on a second bench to make it harder.

plat.e: On your side, resting on your forearm, elbow under your shoulder, feet stacked. Lift your hips until you form a straight line from ankles to shoulders, and hold while breathing.
err: Letting the hips gradually sink.
Tipping the torso forward.
Holding your breath.
plat.p: Complements the front plank by training resistance to side bending. Thirty seconds per side is enough before considering longer.

crp.e: Kneeling with your back to the high pulley, rope held near your face. Curl your spine down, bringing your ribs toward your pelvis, without bending at the hips, then come back up under control.
err: Bending from the hips instead of curling the back.
Pulling with the arms.
Using momentum to come back up.
crp.p: The only ab exercise where you can really add load, and therefore apply progressive overload. Valuable for that reason.

cr.e: Lying down, knees bent, hands on your temples without pulling on your neck. Lift your shoulder blades by curling your upper back, breathe out on the way up, then lower without fully resting your head.
err: Pulling on the neck with the hands.
Lifting the whole torso, which works the hip flexors.
Going fast and bouncing off the floor.
cr.p: Move to a slower range rather than more reps. Beyond twenty-five, add a weight on your chest.

sup.e: Lying face down, arms straight in front. Lift your chest and thighs off the floor at the same time while squeezing your glutes, hold a few seconds, then lower under control.
err: Lifting by craning the neck backward.
Lifting only the arms.
Holding your breath.
sup.p: Lower back strengthening you can do anywhere, with no bench or weight. Useful early in the cycle before moving on to bench back extensions.

corde.e: Elbows close to your body, the rotation comes from the wrists, not the shoulders. Low jumps, just a few centimetres, landing softly on the balls of your feet.
err: Jumping too high, which tires you out for nothing.
Turning the rope with your whole arms.
Landing on your heels.
corde.p: The most time-efficient cardio, but demanding on the calves and Achilles tendons. Start with thirty-second blocks.

enf.e: Kneeling, hips toward your heels, arms stretched far in front, forehead toward the floor. Relax your shoulders and breathe slowly, letting your rib cage open with each breath in.
err: Forcing through the shoulders instead of letting your weight sink.
Holding your breath.
Lifting your hips off your heels.
enf.p: Do it at the end of a workout or the next day. No effort target, just time spent in the position.

mol.e: Balls of your feet on the machine step, heels hanging off. Lower your heels as far as possible until you feel the stretch, pause, then rise onto your toes, pausing at the top too.
err: Bouncing at the bottom without holding the stretch, which works the tendon rather than the muscle.
Cutting the rise short and never reaching full extension.
Bending the knees, which shifts the work onto the soleus.
mol.p: Calves respond to time under tension more than to load. A one-second stop at the bottom and top beats ten more kilos.

molA.e: Seated, knees bent at 90° under the pad, balls of your feet on the step. Lower your heels, then push up onto your toes without lifting your thighs off the pad.
err: Helping with your hands by pushing on the pad.
Going fast and losing range.
Neglecting the stretch at the bottom.
molA.p: With the knee bent, the soleus does the work, under the gastrocnemius. Complementary to the standing version, not redundant.

molP.e: Standing on a step, balls of your feet on the edge, heels hanging off. Lower slowly, then rise onto your toes, one leg at a time if it's too easy.
err: Holding on firmly and taking body weight off with your arms.
Rushing through without control.
Staying in a shortened range.
molP.p: Switch to one leg when twenty reps come easily, rather than adding more.

shr.e: Standing, bar at arm's length in front of your thighs, arms straight and relaxed. Raise your shoulders straight up toward your ears, pause at the top, then lower under control.
err: Rolling the shoulders, which is pointless and stressful for the joint.
Bending the arms to help.
Cutting the descent short and losing the stretch.
shr.p: The traps can handle heavy loads but need range of motion. If your shoulders no longer rise clearly, it's too heavy.

shrH.e: A dumbbell in each hand by your sides, arms straight. Raise your shoulders straight up, pause for one second, then lower slowly.
err: Pushing the head forward on the way up.
Using momentum from the legs.
Skipping the pause at the top.
shrH.p: Dumbbells allow a freer range than the bar, which bumps into your thighs. A good choice if you feel wrist discomfort.

tir.e: Bar in front of your thighs, shoulder-width grip. Pull the bar up along your body, leading with your elbows, to chest height, then lower under control.
err: Pulling above the chest, which pinches the shoulder.
Using too narrow a grip, which makes that stress worse.
Swinging the torso to lift the bar.
tir.p: A movement to watch if your shoulders are sensitive: stop at chest height and don't push it if it pinches. Shrugs are a safer alternative.

poi.e: Seated, forearms resting on your thighs or a bench, palms up, wrists hanging off. Let the bar roll to your fingertips, then close your hand and curl your wrist up.
err: Lifting the forearms off the support.
Skipping the phase where the bar rolls into the fingers, which trains your grip.
Going heavy on a fragile joint.
poi.p: Long sets, fifteen to twenty reps. The forearm is made of small, endurance-oriented muscles that don't respond to heavy loads.

poiI.e: Same position, but palms down. Let your wrist drop, then raise it without moving your forearm.
err: Using the same weight as palms up: the extensors are much weaker.
Moving the elbow.
Going fast.
poiI.p: Often the remedy for outer elbow pain in people who do a lot of pulling. Very light, very controlled.

ferm.e: A heavy dumbbell in each hand, shoulders down and back, torso upright. Walk with steady steps over a set distance without letting your shoulders sag.
err: Leaning the torso forward.
Taking strides that are too long, which throws off your balance.
Letting go before finishing the distance: better lighter and farther.
ferm.p: Trains grip, core and traps at the same time. An excellent addition if your grip gives out before your back on the deadlift.

add.e: Seated, thighs spread against the pads. Squeeze your legs together under control, pause, then let them return slowly without letting the weight slam.
err: Letting the weight return in free fall, which yanks on the groin.
Looking for an excessive spread.
Helping with your hands on the pads.
add.p: Often mocked, often useful: adductors are frequently injured in pivoting sports. Keep it light and controlled.

sumo.e: Feet very wide, toes turned out, one dumbbell held with both hands between your legs. Descend keeping your torso upright and knees in line with your feet, then stand up by pushing the floor away.
err: Letting the knees cave inward.
Leaning the torso forward.
Spreading the feet so wide you can no longer go down.
sumo.p: An alternative to the adductor machine when you don't have one. Unlike the machine, it also works the glutes.

molh.e: A dumbbell in each hand, arms by your sides, balls of your feet on a step or plate with heels hanging off. Lower your heels as far as your ankle allows, pause at the bottom, then rise onto your toes and hold one second at the top.
err: Bouncing at the bottom without holding the stretch, which works the tendon rather than the muscle.
Bending the knees to help, which turns it into a mini squat.
molh.p: Calves respond to time under tension more than to load. Aim for 12 to 20 slow reps before going up one dumbbell.

molp.e: Seated in the leg press, legs almost straight, place only the balls of your feet at the bottom of the platform. Push with your toes by extending your ankle, then let the weight lower your heel to the stretch.
err: Keeping the machine's safety engaged, which blocks the range of motion.
Fully straightening the knee and locking it under load.
molp.p: This is the variation that allows the most load without needing balance. Useful if your calves tire before your feet on standing versions.

mol1.e: Standing on a step, ball of one foot on the edge, other leg raised, one hand on the wall for balance. Lower your heel as far as possible, then rise onto your toes and hold for one second.
err: Pulling on the wall with your arm, which removes half the load.
Cutting the range short at the bottom because the stretch pulls.
mol1.p: Body weight on one leg is enough for a long time. Once you pass 20 clean reps, hold a dumbbell in your free hand.

elp.e: Low pulley, handle in the opposite hand, cable passing in front of your legs. Raise your arm out to the side to horizontal, elbow very slightly bent, little finger slightly higher than the thumb. Control the descent without letting the cable pull you.
err: Raising above horizontal, which shifts the work onto the trap.
Using a push from the legs to start the arm.
elp.p: Unlike dumbbells, the cable keeps tension at the bottom of the movement. Light load, long sets: 12 to 20 reps.

scap.e: Standing, a light dumbbell in each hand, palms facing each other. Raise your arms diagonally, about 30° in front of your shoulders, to shoulder height: your arms form a Y. Lower slowly.
err: Going too heavy, which makes you shrug and removes the point of the movement.
Raising straight out to the side, which turns it into a regular lateral raise.
scap.p: This diagonal plane is the most comfortable for the shoulder. A good first shoulder exercise if lateral raises pinch.

dbug.e: Lying on your back, arms straight toward the ceiling, knees bent above your hips. Press your lower back into the floor and keep it there. Slowly lower one arm and the opposite leg toward the floor without touching, then come back and alternate.
err: Letting the lower back arch as soon as the leg goes down: that's the signal to stop, not a detail.
Going fast, when the whole point is in the slowness.
dbug.p: Progress by going lower and slower, not by adding reps. If your back lifts off, you've gone too far.

pal.e: Standing side-on to a cable set at chest height, both hands on the handle against your sternum, feet apart. Press your arms out in front of you and resist the rotation the cable pulls you into. Hold two seconds with arms straight, come back.
err: Letting the torso rotate toward the cable, which cancels all the work.
Going heavy: past a certain point you stop resisting and compensate with your hips.
pal.p: Progress by stepping farther from the cable rather than adding load. It's the best core exercise for people who find planks boring.

rkp.e: Bar resting on the safety pins of a rack, at knee height. Shoulder-width grip, back flat, chest open. Pull by driving your hips forward until you're fully upright, then set the bar back on the pins without dropping it.
err: Rounding the upper back at the start, which puts everything on the discs.
Pulling with the arms instead of driving with the hips.
rkp.p: The shorter range lets you go heavier than a full deadlift: that's the point, but also the trap. Capped at RPE 8; technique breaks down fast on this exercise.

lomsol.e: Lying face down, hands by your temples, feet held or anchored. Lift your torso by contracting your lower back and glutes until your chest leaves the floor, then lower without fully relaxing.
err: Lifting as high as possible by arching, when a few centimetres are enough.
Pulling on the neck with the hands.
lomsol.p: No equipment needed, it's the fallback version of the back extension bench. When 15 reps come easily, hold two seconds at the top of each rep.

tirp.e: Low pulley, short bar in an overhand shoulder-width grip. Pull your elbows up and out, the bar travelling along your torso to chest height. Your elbows always stay higher than your hands. Lower under control.
err: Pulling up to the chin, which puts the shoulder in extreme internal rotation.
Using too narrow a grip, which makes the pinching worse.
tirp.p: Stop at chest height, no higher: that's where the benefit-to-risk ratio is good. If the shoulder pinches anywhere, cut the range before cutting the load.

poih.e: Seated, forearms on your thighs, palms up, wrists hanging past your knees. Let the dumbbells roll to your fingertips, then close your hand and curl your wrist up.
err: Lifting the forearm off the thigh to help.
Using a minimal range, when rolling through the fingertips is exactly the useful part.
poih.p: Light load and long sets, 15 to 25 reps. The forearm handles volume better than load.

poiinv.e: Forearms on a bench or your thighs, palms down, wrists hanging off. Let your hand drop under its own weight, then raise the back of your hand toward the ceiling without moving your forearm.
err: Using the same weight as the palms-up version: the extensors are much weaker.
Moving the elbow to compensate.
poiinv.p: The side almost nobody trains, and the one that protects the elbow when the outside of it hurts. Very light, very clean, 15 to 20 reps.

addsol.e: Lying on your side, bottom leg straight, top leg bent and placed in front. Raise the straight bottom leg toward the ceiling with the foot flat, then lower without fully resting it.
err: Rolling the pelvis back to gain range.
Going fast: the muscle is small, control is everything.
addsol.p: No equipment, useful to catch up a weak inner thigh. When 20 reps per side come easily, add a band around your ankles.

sqlat.e: Bar on your traps, feet very wide, toes slightly turned out. Shift your weight onto one leg by bending that knee, while the other leg stays straight and its inner thigh stretches. Come back to the centre and alternate.
err: Letting the bent knee cave inward.
Spreading the feet wider than your flexibility allows, which tips the pelvis.
sqlat.p: Start with an empty bar to find the stance that suits you. It's one of the few exercises that loads the adductor in a lengthened position, where injuries happen.

ois.e: Torso bent at 45° or more, back flat, a light dumbbell in each hand, arms hanging. Raise your arms out to the side leading with the elbows, until your hands reach shoulder height. Squeeze your shoulder blades at the top, lower slowly.
err: Going too heavy, which turns the movement into a row.
Rounding the back, which tires the lower back before the shoulder.
ois.p: The rear delt is small: 12 to 20 reps with ridiculously light dumbbells do more than a load you have to swing.

crinv.e: Lying on your back, hands by your sides or gripping something behind your head, knees bent. Curl your pelvis toward your chest, lifting your lower back off the floor, knees toward your face, then lower slowly without letting your feet touch.
err: Swinging the legs to build momentum, which works the hip joint rather than the abs.
Dropping down all at once.
crinv.p: What matters is the pelvic curl, not how high the legs go. Slow the descent before adding reps.

russ.e: Seated, knees bent, heels on the floor or slightly raised, torso leaning back at 45°. Hands together in front of your chest, rotate your torso to one side then the other, keeping the angle of your back constant.
err: Moving only the arms while the torso stays still.
Rounding the back and slumping, which puts the load on the lower back.
russ.p: Keep the torso leaning back from start to finish: as soon as it straightens, the exercise becomes easy and useless. Next step, a light dumbbell in your hands.

pont.e: Lying on your back, knees bent, feet flat near your glutes, arms by your sides. Push through your heels and raise your hips until knees, hips and shoulders line up. Squeeze your glutes at the top for a second, lower without fully resting.
err: Rising by arching the lower back instead of squeezing the glutes, which you'll feel right away in your lower back.
Feet too far out, which shifts the work onto the hamstrings.
pont.p: The no-equipment starting point. When 20 reps cost nothing, move to the single-leg bridge, then the loaded hip thrust.

pont1.e: Same position as the glute bridge, but with one leg stretched toward the ceiling. Push through the heel on the floor and raise your hips, keeping both hips at the same height. Squeeze the glute at the top, lower slowly.
err: Letting the hip on the free side sag, which shows a glute that can't hold yet.
Pushing through the toes rather than the heel.
pont1.p: Twice the load of the regular bridge with no equipment at all. If your pelvis tilts, go back to two legs until it holds.

kick.e: Ankle strap, low pulley, facing the machine, hands on the frame, torso leaning slightly forward. Push your leg back by extending your hip, without arching your lower back. Squeeze the glute at the end of the movement, return under control.
err: Chasing range by arching: the movement comes from the hip, not the back.
Bending and straightening the knee, which shifts the work onto the hamstring.
kick.p: This is an isolation exercise, not a loading exercise. Light, 12 to 20 reps per leg, at the end of the workout after a heavy movement.

pth.e: Back to a low pulley, rope passed between your legs, hands holding the ends. Step forward twice, then push your hips back keeping your back flat until you feel the hamstring stretch. Come back by driving your hips forward, glutes squeezed.
err: Pulling with the arms instead of letting the hips do all the work.
Finishing by arching the lower back instead of ending with a glute squeeze.
pth.p: The easiest hip hinge to learn: the cable gives you the direction, you can't cheat for long. Good practice before the Romanian deadlift.

bul.e: A dumbbell in each hand, top of the back foot on a bench, front foot far enough forward. Lower straight down until your front thigh is close to horizontal, back knee toward the floor, then come up by pushing through the front heel.
err: Front foot too close to the bench, which drives the knee forward.
Chasing balance rather than depth: start unloaded, one hand on the wall if needed.
bul.p: Extremely effective and extremely uncomfortable, that's normal. Two extra reps are worth more than one more dumbbell on this exercise.

mont.e: A dumbbell in each hand, facing a knee-height bench. Put your whole foot on it, then step up pushing only with that leg, without pushing off the foot on the floor. Lower the same foot slowly, under control.
err: Pushing off with the bottom leg, which empties the exercise of its point.
Choosing a step that's too high, which forces you to use your torso.
mont.p: The slow descent is half the work. Raise the step height before raising the load, up to about knee height.

sqpc.e: Feet hip-width apart, toes slightly turned out, arms in front for balance. Push your hips back and go as low as your back stays flat, knees in line with your feet. Stand up by pushing through your whole foot.
err: Heels lifting: push your hips back further or widen your stance a little.
Knees caving inward on the way up.
sqpc.p: Use it to build range before adding load. When 20 deep reps come effortlessly, move to the barbell squat or Bulgarian split squats.

fepc.e: Standing, hands on your hips. Take a long step forward and lower until your back knee approaches the floor, torso upright. Come up by pushing through the front leg and go straight into the next step with the other leg.
err: Step too short, which sends the front knee well past the toes.
Torso leaning forward to make up for a lack of balance.
fepc.p: Count reps per leg, not in total. When 12 per leg come out cleanly, hold a dumbbell in each hand.

bfront.e: Lying on a bench, bar held with arms straight above your shoulders, shoulder-width grip. Bend only your elbows to lower the bar toward your forehead or just above it, elbows staying pointed at the ceiling. Come back up by straightening your arms.
err: Letting the elbows flare outward, which takes tension off the triceps.
Moving the shoulders to turn the movement into a press.
bfront.p: If your elbows are sensitive, an EZ bar is much more comfortable than a straight bar. Moderate load: the joint matters more than the number here.

extnh.e: Seated with your back straight, one dumbbell held with both hands overhead, arms straight. Lower the dumbbell behind your head by bending only your elbows, which stay tucked forward. Lower to the stretch, then press up.
err: Flaring the elbows wide, which loses the stretch that is precisely the point of the overhead position.
Arching the lower back to help the press.
extnh.p: With your arms overhead, you stretch the triceps' long head, which cable pushdowns work poorly. Keep it in the program as a complement, not a replacement.

kickt.e: Torso bent to horizontal, one hand resting on a bench, dumbbell in the other hand, elbow raised to torso level and locked there. Extend your arm back to full extension, squeeze for a second, return slowly.
err: Letting the elbow drop, which replaces the extension with a shoulder swing.
Going heavy: past a few kilos, the movement becomes impossible to keep clean.
kickt.p: A light finishing exercise, 12 to 20 reps. The squeeze at the end of the movement is all it has to offer, so make it count.

curlp.e: Low pulley, short bar in an underhand grip, standing one step from the machine. Elbows pinned to your torso and still, curl the bar to your shoulders, then lower slowly to full elbow extension.
err: Leaning back to swing the weight up.
Moving the elbows forward at the top, which lets the biceps rest.
curlp.p: The cable keeps tension from start to finish, unlike dumbbells, which are light at the bottom. Useful at the end of a workout, in sets of 12 to 15.

dmm.e: Seated, back pressed against the backrest, handles at shoulder height. Press straight up until your arms are almost straight without locking your elbows, then lower until your hands come back to shoulder height.
err: Lifting your back off the backrest to press heavier.
Lowering the handles well below the shoulders, which puts the joint in a vulnerable position.
dmm.p: The machine holds the path for you, which lets you get closer to failure safely. A good choice if the standing press makes you arch.

velo.e: Set the saddle at hip height, leg almost straight at the bottom of the pedal stroke. Five minutes of easy warm-up, then alternate 40 seconds fast and 80 seconds easy, and finish with three minutes of cool-down.
err: Saddle too low, which crushes the knee on every pedal stroke.
Staying seated and pulling on the handlebars when the resistance goes up.
velo.p: Cycling has no impact on the ground, making it the easiest cardio to fit alongside a strength program without hurting leg recovery. Increase resistance before duration.

scappu.e: Hanging from a bar, arms straight, shoulders relaxed up toward your ears. Without bending your elbows, pull your shoulders down and bring your shoulder blades together: your body rises only a few centimetres. Hold one second at the top, release slowly.
err: Bending the elbows, which turns it into a short pull-up instead of shoulder blade work.
Chasing range: a few centimetres is enough, that's normal.
scappu.p: The only traps and shoulder blade exercise that needs just a bar. It's also the best preparation if full pull-ups aren't there yet: 3 sets of 8 before each back workout.

pompe.e: Feet on a bench or chair, hands on the floor slightly wider than your shoulders, body in a line. The higher your feet, the more the load shifts to the upper chest and shoulders. Lower your chest toward the floor, elbows going back, then push.
err: Hips sagging once the feet are raised, which your lower back pays for.
Raising the feet too high at once: start at chair height.
pompe.p: This is how you keep progressing on push-ups without equipment: raise your feet before adding reps, then add weight on your back.

pecdk.e: Seated with your back pressed against the backrest, set the seat so the handles are at chest height. Elbows slightly bent and fixed, bring your arms together in front of you while squeezing your chest, pause, then return slowly until you feel the stretch.
err: Lifting your back off the backrest to push with your shoulders.
Letting the arms go too far back on the return, which puts the shoulder at risk.
Bending the elbows along the way, which turns the fly into a press.
pecdk.p: An isolation machine: feel comes before load. Add a plate when all 15 reps come out with a clean pause with arms closed.

chpm.e: Set the seat so the handles are level with the middle of your chest. Shoulder blades squeezed against the backrest, press forward without violently locking your elbows, then return under control to the stretch.
err: Seat too low, which makes you press upward and loads the shoulders.
Lifting the shoulder blades off the backrest at the end of the press.
Letting the handles come back all at once.
chpm.p: The guided path lets you get closer to failure safely: a good exercise to finish a push workout. Increase the load when you go past the top of the rep range.

ecah.e: Lying on a flat bench, dumbbells above your chest, palms facing each other, elbows very slightly bent. Open your arms in an arc until you feel your chest stretch, without going below bench level, then close while squeezing.
err: Lowering the elbows too far, which pulls on the front of the shoulder.
Bending the elbows a lot to lift heavier.
Clanking the dumbbells at the top, which releases the tension.
ecah.p: Light load, controlled range. Tension disappears at the top: stop the movement a little before the dumbbells touch.

ecai.e: Bench inclined at 30°, dumbbells above your chest, elbows slightly bent. Open your arms in an arc until you feel your upper chest stretch, then close keeping the same elbow bend.
err: Inclining the bench to 45° or more, which hands the work to the shoulders.
Going lower than the shoulder comfortably allows.
Turning the movement into a press by bending the elbows.
ecai.p: A good complement to the flat bench press. Stay at a load that lets you feel the stretch without pain at the front of the shoulder.

ecab.e: Between two low pulleys, a handle in each hand, one step forward. Elbows slightly bent, bring your hands from low to high in front of you up to shoulder height, squeezing your upper chest, then lower slowly.
err: Raising the hands above the shoulders, which shifts the work to the delts.
Pulling with the biceps by bending the elbows.
Leaning back to swing the weight.
ecab.p: The cable keeps tension throughout the movement. Work in sets of 12 to 15 and increase the load in small steps.

rwapp.e: Lying face down on a bench inclined at 30-45°, chest supported, a dumbbell in each hand, arms straight. Pull your elbows up and back while squeezing your shoulder blades, pause, then lower under control.
err: Lifting your chest off the bench to cheat with your torso.
Shrugging toward your ears instead of squeezing the shoulder blades.
Pulling only with the arms without bringing the shoulder blades together.
rwapp.p: The bench supports your torso: no stress on the lower back. It's the row to choose if your lower back bothers you. Go up in dumbbells when the last rep still keeps the pause.

tbar.e: Straddling the bar, one end wedged in a corner or holder, V-handle under the plates. Knees bent, torso bent at 45°, back flat. Pull the handle to your lower chest while squeezing your shoulder blades, then lower to straight arms.
err: Rounding the lower back under the load.
Straightening the torso on each rep to swing the bar.
Pulling toward the neck rather than the lower chest.
tbar.p: Lets you load the back heavily with a simple bar path. If your lower back tires before your back muscles, replace it with the chest-supported row.

rwm.e: Seated, chest against the pad, set the seat so the handles are level with your lower chest. Pull your elbows back while squeezing your shoulder blades, pause, then release slowly to a full back stretch.
err: Lifting your chest off the pad to pull with your torso.
Cutting the return short and losing the stretch.
Shrugging while pulling.
rwm.p: A guided path, easy to load and push close to failure. Remember to stretch your back on every return: that's half the work.

tbt.e: Facing a high pulley, bar in hand, arms straight in front of you, torso leaning slightly. Elbows almost locked, bring the bar down in an arc to your thighs, thinking about pulling with your back, then let it rise slowly.
err: Bending the elbows, which turns the movement into a triceps extension.
Leaning further and further to bring the bar down.
Letting the bar shoot back up.
tbt.p: Isolates the lats without the biceps: ideal for learning to feel your back before pull-ups. Work in sets of 12 to 15.

pull.e: Lying on a bench, one dumbbell held with both hands above your chest, elbows slightly bent. Lower the dumbbell behind your head in an arc until you feel your back and chest stretch, then bring it back over your chest.
err: Going too low, beyond your shoulder flexibility.
Bending and straightening the elbows during the movement.
Arching the back hard to gain range.
pull.p: As much a stretching exercise as a strength one: keep the load moderate and control the descent. Stop the range as soon as your shoulders pull.

oisp.e: Between two pulleys set at shoulder height, cables crossed, left handle in your right hand and vice versa. Arms almost straight, open your arms backward at shoulder height, then return slowly.
err: Squeezing the shoulder blades as hard as possible, which hands the work to the traps.
Pulling with the arms by bending the elbows.
Loading too heavy for this small muscle.
oisp.p: The rear delt responds to long sets: 15 to 20 reps, light load. A good counterweight to all the pressing exercises.

pp.e: Standing, bar resting on your upper chest, grip slightly wider than your shoulders. Bend your knees slightly, then drive with your legs and follow through by pressing the bar overhead, arms straight. Lower the bar to your chest under control.
err: Bending the knees too low, which turns it into a squat.
Arching the back at the end of the press.
Letting the bar crash onto your chest.
pp.p: Leg drive lets you handle more weight than the overhead press. It's a strength and power exercise, in short sets of 3 to 6.

dcs.e: Lying on the bench, hands shoulder-width apart on the bar, shoulder blades squeezed. Lower the bar to your lower chest keeping your elbows close to your body, then press by straightening your arms.
err: Grip too narrow, hands touching, which hurts the wrists.
Elbows flaring, which takes the work away from the triceps.
Bouncing off the chest.
dcs.p: Capped at RPE 8, like the bench press: without a spotter, keep two reps in reserve. It's the go-to heavy exercise for the triceps.

dipm.e: Seated, back against the backrest, handles in hand beside your torso. Push down until your arms are straight, without lifting your back, then come up under control until your elbows form a right angle.
err: Coming up too high, which stretches the front of the shoulder.
Leaning the torso forward to help.
Locking the elbows violently.
dipm.p: A guided version of dips, for those who can't lift their body weight yet. Increase the load when you go past 12 clean reps.

curlc.e: Seated on a bench, legs apart, elbow resting against your inner thigh, dumbbell in hand, arm straight. Curl the dumbbell toward your shoulder without moving your elbow, squeeze the biceps at the top, then lower slowly to full extension.
err: Lifting the elbow off the thigh to swing the dumbbell.
Not lowering all the way.
Twisting the torso to help the lift.
curlc.p: Bracing against the thigh prevents any cheating. Work slowly, especially on the way down. Light load, maximum feel.

martc.e: Facing a low pulley, rope in hand, palms facing each other. Elbows pinned to your body, curl the rope toward your shoulders keeping your wrists neutral, then lower slowly.
err: Moving the elbows forward on the way up.
Swinging the torso to lift the weight.
Bending the wrists at the end of the movement.
martc.p: The neutral grip works the brachialis and forearms on top of the biceps. Constant tension thanks to the cable: sets of 10 to 15.

zott.e: Standing, a dumbbell in each hand, palms facing forward. Curl up like a regular curl, rotate your wrists at the top so your palms face down, then lower slowly in that position. Turn your palms back up at the bottom before the next rep.
err: Lowering too fast, when the palms-down descent is what works the forearms.
Swinging the torso.
Choosing a load based on the lift, too heavy for the descent.
zott.p: Choose the load for the weakest phase, the palms-down descent. Count three seconds on the way down.

hack.e: Back and shoulders pressed against the pads, feet hip-width apart in the middle of the platform. Release the safety, lower until your thighs are at least parallel to the platform, then push without locking your knees.
err: Lifting the lower back off at the bottom of the descent.
Placing the feet too low on the platform, which overloads the knees.
Cutting the range short to load heavier.
hack.p: The back is supported: you can push the quads close to failure without lower back risk. Excellent alongside or instead of the barbell squat.

smith.e: Bar on your upper back, feet slightly in front of the bar, shoulder-width apart. Unrack the bar, descend by pushing your hips back to parallel, then come up by pushing through your heels.
err: Placing the feet under the bar, which pushes the knees too far forward.
Rounding the lower back at the bottom of the movement.
Forgetting to re-lock the bar on the hooks at the end of the set.
smith.p: The guided path lets you train without a spotter. Loads aren't comparable to the free squat: start over with benchmarks specific to this machine.

gob.e: Standing, one dumbbell held vertically against your chest, elbows pointing down. Feet slightly wider than your hips, sit down between your heels, torso upright, until your elbows brush the inside of your knees. Stand up by pushing the floor away.
err: Letting the dumbbell drift away from the chest, which tips the torso forward.
Knees caving inward on the way up.
Heels lifting at the bottom.
gob.p: The best squat for learning the position, and the simplest at home. When the heaviest dumbbell becomes too light, move to the barbell squat or slow the descent.

rmh.e: Standing, a dumbbell in each hand in front of your thighs, knees slightly bent and fixed. Push your hips back letting the dumbbells slide down your legs, back flat, to the hamstring stretch, then come back by driving your hips forward.
err: Rounding the back to go lower.
Bending the knees on the way down.
Letting the dumbbells drift away from the legs.
rmh.p: The same movement as the barbell Romanian deadlift, accessible with dumbbells. Stop the descent where your back would start to round, not at the floor.

sdts.e: Feet very wide, toes turned out, bar over the middle of your feet. Grip the bar between your legs, arms straight, chest out, back flat. Push the floor away while spreading your knees, and finish standing with your glutes squeezed.
err: Letting the knees cave inward.
Raising the hips before the bar, which turns it into a stiff-legged deadlift.
Rounding the back at the start.
sdts.p: Capped at RPE 8, like the conventional deadlift. The more upright torso spares the lower back: a good option if the conventional one bothers you.

trap.e: Standing in the centre of the hex bar, feet hip-width apart. Lower by bending your hips and knees, grab the handles, back flat, chest out. Push the floor away to stand up, then lower the bar under control.
err: Rounding the back at the bottom.
Letting the hips rise faster than the shoulders.
Letting go of the bar on the floor between reps.
trap.p: The load stays in line with your body: it's the most accessible deadlift and the gentlest on the back. Capped at RPE 8. Requires a trap bar.

abd.e: Seated, back against the backrest, pads against the outside of your knees. Spread your legs as far as you can under control, pause, then return slowly without letting the plates touch.
err: Jerking to start the weight.
Returning too fast and letting the plates slam.
Cutting the range short.
abd.p: The glute medius stabilises the pelvis on every step and in the squat. Long sets of 15 to 20, with a pause with legs apart.

nord.e: Kneeling on a pad, ankles locked under a support or held by a partner. Body straight from knees to shoulders, let yourself fall forward as slowly as possible while resisting with your hamstrings, catch yourself with your hands, then push back up.
err: Breaking at the hips instead of keeping your body straight.
Dropping all at once instead of braking the descent.
Doing too many reps at first: the exercise is very demanding.
nord.p: One of the most effective exercises for the hamstrings and injury prevention. Start with 3 to 5 slow descents; the way back up will come with time.

roue.e: Kneeling, wheel held with both hands under your shoulders. Pelvis tucked and glutes squeezed, roll the wheel out in front of you as far as you can without arching your lower back, then come back by pulling with your abs.
err: Arching the lower back by going too far.
Coming back by pushing your hips back instead of contracting your abs.
Going all the way to the floor in the first sessions.
roue.p: Range is earned gradually: stop where your back would start to arch. Requires an ab wheel, a small and cheap accessory.

rgen.e: Supported on your forearms or hands at a dip station, back against the backrest, legs hanging. Raise your knees toward your chest by curling your pelvis, then lower slowly without swinging.
err: Swinging the legs to build momentum.
Raising the knees without curling the pelvis, which only works the hips.
Letting the legs drop.
rgen.p: A more accessible version of hanging leg raises. When 15 reps come out, gradually straighten your legs.

mclimb.e: In push-up position, hands under your shoulders, core braced. Bring one knee toward your chest, then quickly alternate legs as if running, keeping your hips at shoulder height.
err: Pushing the hips up in the air.
Letting the shoulders drift far in front of the hands.
Sacrificing core stability for speed.
mclimb.p: Core work and cardio at once. Start with 20 to 30 clean seconds; only add time if your hips stay stable.

ellip.e: Feet flat on the pedals, hands on the moving handles. Five minutes of easy warm-up, then alternate 1 minute hard and 1 minute easy, and finish with three minutes of cool-down.
err: Leaning your whole weight on the handles.
Setting the resistance so low that the movement becomes momentum.
ellip.p: No impact on the joints: ideal for cardio if your knees bother you. Increase resistance before duration.

stair.e: Step onto the stairs, torso upright, hands resting lightly on the rails. Start at a moderate pace for five minutes, then alternate 1 minute faster and 1 minute easy.
err: Hanging on the rails, which takes all the work away from the legs.
Leaning far forward.
Climbing on your toes.
stair.p: Demanding cardio that also works the glutes. Schedule it away from leg workouts so it doesn't hurt recovery.

tapis.e: Five minutes of brisk walking to warm up, then run at a comfortable pace, short strides, torso upright. For intervals, alternate 1 minute fast and 2 minutes slow, and finish with three minutes of walking.
err: Holding the rails while running.
Taking long strides that land on the heel.
Starting too fast without a warm-up.
tapis.p: A 1% incline makes up for the lack of air resistance. Increase duration before speed.

wgs.e: In a forward lunge, hand on the front leg's side placed on the floor. Lower your elbow toward the inside of your ankle, then open your arm toward the ceiling by rotating your torso and following your hand with your eyes. Come back and repeat, then switch sides.
err: Letting the back knee collapse to the floor.
Turning only the arm without opening the upper back.
Rushing instead of holding each position.
wgs.p: One movement for the hips, upper back and shoulders: perfect as a warm-up. Five slow reps per side.

ischs.e: Lying on your back, a strap or towel around your foot. Raise the straight leg until you feel the stretch at the back of the thigh, the other leg staying on the floor. Hold the position while breathing, then switch sides.
err: Bending the knee of the stretched leg.
Lifting the pelvis or the leg on the floor.
Pulling in jerks.
ischs.p: Do it after the workout or in the evening, never cold before a deadlift. Hold 45 seconds per leg, without looking for pain.

kbsw.e: Feet slightly wider than your hips, kettlebell on the floor in front of you. Grab it with one hand, back flat, and hike it between your legs. Then snap your hips forward to swing it up to chest height, arm relaxed, and let it swing back between your legs as you push your hips back.
err: Lifting with the arm or shoulders instead of driving with the hips.
Bending the knees like a squat instead of pushing the hips back.
Rounding the back at the bottom of the movement.
kbsw.p: It's an explosive hip movement, not a shoulder exercise: the kettlebell floats, the glutes do the work. Sets of 10 to 15 per arm, switching hands each set.

kbfs.e: A kettlebell in each hand in the rack position: handles in front of your collarbones, elbows tucked against your torso. Feet shoulder-width apart, squat down with your torso upright to parallel, then come up by pushing through your heels.
err: Letting the elbows flare and the kettlebells pull the torso forward.
Heels lifting at the bottom.
Letting the knees cave inward.
kbfs.p: Holding the load in front forces you to keep your torso upright: excellent for the core as much as the legs. Move up in kettlebells when you go past 12 clean reps.

kbsdt1.e: Standing on one leg, kettlebell in the opposite hand. Standing knee slightly bent, tip your torso forward while extending the other leg behind you, back flat, until your torso is almost horizontal. Come back by squeezing the glute of the standing leg.
err: Opening the hip and rotating the pelvis to the side.
Rounding the back to go lower.
Rushing to find your balance instead of controlling.
kbsdt1.p: Works each leg separately and fixes imbalances. Start light: balance limits you before strength. Hold a wall with your other hand at first if needed.

kbdm.e: Standing, a kettlebell in each hand in the rack position, wrists straight. Squeeze your glutes and abs, then press both kettlebells overhead until your arms are straight. Lower under control to your shoulders.
err: Arching the lower back to press.
Bending the wrists backward.
Pushing the kettlebells forward instead of straight up.
kbdm.p: The kettlebell sits behind the wrist, which demands more stability than a dumbbell. If both together are too heavy, alternate one arm then the other.

kbfp.e: Lying on the floor, knees bent, kettlebell held in one hand above your chest, arm straight. Lower it until your elbow touches the floor, pause, then press back toward the ceiling.
err: Letting the elbow bounce off the floor.
Flaring the elbow to 90° from the torso.
Letting the wrist bend under the weight.
kbfp.p: The floor limits the range and protects the shoulder: it's the press to do without a bench. Do both arms before resting.

kbrw.e: One foot forward, torso bent at 45° with your free hand on your front knee, back flat. Kettlebell in the other hand, arm straight. Pull your elbow toward your hip while squeezing your shoulder blade, then lower slowly.
err: Twisting the torso to swing the weight.
Pulling toward the shoulder rather than the hip.
Rounding the back.
kbrw.p: The basic pull at home. When 12 reps come easily, slow the descent to three seconds before changing kettlebells.

kbhp.e: Feet very wide, toes turned out, kettlebell on the floor between your feet. Grab it with both hands, back flat, then stand up explosively, pulling the kettlebell to your sternum, elbows high and out. Lower under control.
err: Pulling only with the arms without leg drive.
Raising the elbows above the shoulders.
Rounding the back at the start.
kbhp.p: An explosive movement linking the legs and upper back. Stick to sets of 8 to 12, keeping the speed on every rep.

kbtgu.e: Lying on your back, kettlebell held with your arm straight above your shoulder, knee on the same side bent. Without ever taking your eyes off the kettlebell, roll onto your elbow, then your hand, lift your hips, sweep the straight leg under you and finish standing. Retrace the path in reverse.
err: Letting the loaded arm bend or drift back.
Rushing through the steps without a stable position between each.
Starting too heavy.
kbtgu.p: An exercise of coordination and shoulder stability more than strength. Learn it first unloaded, with a shoe balanced on your fist, then with a light kettlebell. One to three reps per side is enough.

kbwm.e: Kettlebell held with your arm straight overhead, feet turned 45° to the opposite side. Look at the kettlebell and push the hip on the loaded side out, then slide your other hand down your leg to the floor or your shin. Come back up keeping the arm vertical.
err: Bending the loaded arm.
Rotating the torso toward the floor instead of tilting it sideways.
Going lower than your hamstring flexibility allows.
kbwm.p: Works the obliques, hip mobility and shoulder stability in one movement. Start unloaded, then light: 5 slow reps per side.

kbthr.e: Kettlebells in the rack position in front of your shoulders. Squat down with your torso upright, then drive up in one go and use the leg drive to press the kettlebells overhead. Bring them back to your shoulders as you start the next squat.
err: Doing the squat then the press in two separate steps, without linking them.
Letting the torso fall forward at the bottom.
Arching the back at the end of the press.
kbthr.p: A full-body exercise that's very demanding on cardio: perfect for a conditioning-focused bonus workout. Sets of 8 to 12 at a steady pace.

elpa.e: Standing, band held with both hands in front of you at shoulder height, arms straight, hands shoulder-width apart. Spread your arms out to the sides until the band touches your chest, squeezing your shoulder blades, then return slowly.
err: Bending the elbows to make the movement easier.
Shrugging toward the ears.
Letting the band snap back.
elpa.p: Ideal as a warm-up before a push workout, and for posture. Sets of 15 to 25; bring your hands closer on the band to make it harder.

elrot.e: Band anchored at elbow height to your side. Elbow pinned to your body and bent at 90°, forearm in front of your belly. Rotate your forearm outward without lifting your elbow, then return slowly.
err: Lifting the elbow off the body.
Rotating the torso to help the movement.
Choosing a band that's too strong.
elrot.p: Strengthens the small muscles that stabilise the shoulder: a good investment against pain when pressing. Sets of 15 to 20, light resistance.

eldm.e: Standing on the band, feet hip-width apart, handles at shoulder height. Press your hands overhead until your arms are straight, then lower slowly to your shoulders.
err: Arching the back to finish the press.
Letting the elbows drift far forward.
Dropping back down all at once.
eldm.p: Resistance increases as the band stretches: the top of the movement is the hardest. Widen your stance on the band to increase tension.

elel.e: Standing on the band, a handle in each hand by your thighs. Raise your arms out to the sides to horizontal, elbows very slightly bent, then lower slowly.
err: Raising above horizontal.
Shrugging the shoulders.
Swinging the torso.
elel.p: Long sets of 15 to 20. For more resistance, shorten the band by holding it lower.

elec.e: Band anchored behind you at chest height, a handle in each hand, arms open. Elbows slightly bent and fixed, bring your hands together in front of you while squeezing your chest, then return slowly.
err: Bending the elbows, which turns the fly into a press.
Moving the torso forward instead of closing the arms.
Letting the arms go too far back.
elec.p: The home equivalent of the cable fly. Step forward to increase tension.

elsq.e: Standing on the band, feet shoulder-width apart, handles held at shoulder level. Squat down, torso upright, to parallel, then stand up by pushing the floor away.
err: Heels lifting.
Letting the knees cave in.
Not going low enough, where the band barely resists.
elsq.p: The band adds resistance at the top of the movement, where the bodyweight squat gets too easy. Double the band when 20 reps come out.

elgm.e: Standing on the band, the other end looped behind your neck. Knees slightly bent, push your hips back and tip your torso forward, back flat, to the hamstring stretch, then stand back up by driving your hips forward.
err: Rounding the back.
Bending the knees to go lower.
Craning the head up into hyperextension.
elgm.p: Teaches the hip hinge with no risk. Sets of 12 to 20, looking for the stretch rather than range.

elpt.e: Back to a low anchor point, band passed between your legs and held with both hands. Push your hips back, letting your hands go between your legs, back flat, then stand up by driving your hips forward and squeezing your glutes.
err: Pulling with the arms instead of driving with the hips.
Squatting instead of pushing the hips back.
Arching the back at the end of the movement.
elpt.p: The equivalent of the cable pull-through. Step farther from the anchor to increase tension.

elmw.e: Mini band around your ankles or above your knees, feet apart, knees slightly bent. Walk forward diagonally in small steps, always keeping the band taut, then walk back the same way.
err: Letting the feet come together and the band go slack.
Standing fully upright, which takes work away from the glutes.
Taking big steps while swaying the hips.
elmw.p: Excellent as a warm-up before legs: it wakes up the glute medius, which stabilises the knee. 10 to 15 steps in each direction.

eladd.e: Band anchored low to your side and looped around the nearest ankle. Standing with that leg out, bring it in front of the other leg, crossing slightly, then return slowly.
err: Leaning the torso to help the movement.
Letting the band yank the leg back.
Turning the foot outward.
eladd.p: Replaces the adductor machine at home. Sets of 15 to 20 per leg.

elmol.e: Standing on the band, handles held at your shoulders, balls of your feet on the band. Rise onto your toes as high as possible, pause, then lower slowly.
err: Bouncing at the bottom of the movement.
Bending the knees.
Only rising halfway.
elmol.p: Put something under the balls of your feet (a step, a book) to gain range. Sets of 15 to 25.

elrm.e: Standing on the band, handles in front of your thighs. Pull your elbows up and out to chest height, hands close to your body, then lower slowly.
err: Raising the elbows above the shoulders.
Grip too narrow, which strains the shoulders.
Swinging the torso.
elrm.p: Stop the movement at chest height: beyond that, the shoulder works in a poor position. Sets of 12 to 15.

eltr.e: Band looped over the pull-up bar, one foot or knee resting in it. Overhand grip slightly wider than your shoulders, pull until your chin clears the bar, then lower to straight arms under control.
err: Dropping at the bottom instead of controlling the descent.
Swinging the legs for momentum.
Only pulling halfway up.
eltr.p: The best path to your first pull-up: gradually switch to thinner bands. Requires a pull-up bar.

curlh.e: Standing, a dumbbell in each hand, arms by your sides, palms facing forward. Elbows pinned to your sides, curl the dumbbells toward your shoulders while turning your wrists slightly outward, squeeze your biceps at the top, then lower slowly to straight arms.
err: Swinging the torso to lift the weight.
Moving the elbows forward at the top, which takes load off the biceps.
Curling back up before straightening the arms at the bottom.
curlh.p: The basic curl, doable anywhere. Work between 8 and 12 reps, controlling the descent over two seconds.

curlez.e: Standing, EZ bar held on the angled parts, palms up, hands shoulder-width apart. Elbows fixed against your sides, curl the bar to your shoulders, then lower under control to straight arms.
err: Using a hip thrust to get the bar moving.
Letting the elbows drift forward.
Cutting the descent short.
curlez.p: The angled bar eases the wrists compared with a straight bar. If your elbows or wrists bother you, this is the version to choose.

spid.e: Lying face down against an incline bench or the vertical side of a preacher bench, arms hanging straight down, EZ bar in hand. Curl the bar by bending your elbows without moving them, squeeze at the top, lower slowly.
err: Lifting your chest off the support to cheat.
Swinging the elbows forward.
Releasing the tension at the bottom.
spid.p: Hanging arms put the biceps under maximum tension at the top of the movement: go lighter than on a standing curl.

pupp.e: Preacher bench placed facing a low pulley, straight or EZ bar attached. Arms flat on the pad, curl the bar toward your chin by bending your elbows, then lower slowly until your arms are almost straight.
err: Lifting the elbows off the pad.
Locking the arms at the bottom and letting the cable pull on the joint.
Standing up from the seat to finish the curl.
pupp.p: The cable keeps constant tension, even at the top. Perfect at the end of a pull workout, between 10 and 15 reps.

pupm.e: Seated at the machine, armpits set against the top of the pad, arms flat. Grab the handles and bend your elbows all the way up, then lower under control until your arms are almost straight.
err: Setting the seat too low, which lifts the arms off the pad.
